subject: food-technology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is the temperature range of the 'danger zone' in which food-poisoning bacteria multiply most rapidly?
options: 0 C to 5 C
5 C to 63 C
63 C to 100 C
-18 C to 0 C
questions.explain: Bacteria multiply most quickly between 5 C and 63 C, so high-risk foods should be kept out of this range.

questions.q: Which of the following is classed as a high-risk food?
options: Cooked rice
Dried pasta
Plain flour
Tinned beans in the unopened tin
questions.explain: Cooked rice is moist and nutrient-rich, making it a high-risk food that can support the growth of bacteria such as Bacillus cereus.

questions.q: What is the recommended temperature for a domestic refrigerator?
options: 0 C to 5 C
8 C to 10 C
10 C to 15 C
questions.explain: A fridge should run between 0 C and 5 C to slow the growth of bacteria on stored food.

questions.q: At what temperature should a freezer be kept?
options: 0 C
5 C
questions.explain: A freezer should be kept at -18 C, at which bacteria become dormant and cannot multiply.

questions.q: What core (centre) temperature should food reach to ensure it is safely cooked?
questions.explain: Food should reach a core temperature of at least 75 C to destroy harmful bacteria.

questions.q: Which condition, alongside food and time, do bacteria need in order to multiply?
options: Warmth
Freezing temperatures
Very dry conditions
Strongly acidic surroundings
questions.explain: Bacteria need warmth, moisture, food and time to multiply, which is why keeping food cold slows their growth.

questions.q: Which type of micro-organism typically appears as a fuzzy growth on the surface of stale bread?
options: Mould
Yeast
Enzyme
Virus
questions.explain: Moulds are micro-organisms that grow as visible fuzzy patches on foods such as bread and cheese.

questions.q: In ideal conditions, roughly how often can a bacterium divide by binary fission?
options: Every 10 to 20 minutes
Every 1 to 2 hours
Every 6 hours
Every 24 hours
questions.explain: In warm, moist conditions bacteria can divide about every 10 to 20 minutes, so numbers rise very quickly.

questions.q: What is meant by 'cross-contamination'?
options: The transfer of harmful bacteria from one food, surface or utensil to another
The browning of fruit when it is cut open
The freezing of food to make it last longer
The addition of preservatives to tinned food
questions.explain: Cross-contamination is the spread of bacteria between foods, hands, equipment or surfaces, often from raw to ready-to-eat food.

questions.q: Why should raw meat be stored on the bottom shelf of the refrigerator?
options: To stop raw juices dripping onto other foods below
Because it is the warmest shelf
So that it freezes more quickly
To keep it within easy reach
questions.explain: Storing raw meat at the bottom prevents its juices dripping onto and contaminating ready-to-eat foods.

questions.q: Why are blue waterproof plasters used to cover cuts in a food kitchen?
options: Blue is not a natural food colour, so a plaster is easily spotted if it falls into food
Blue plasters are cheaper than other colours
Blue plasters help wounds heal faster
Blue plasters are the only ones that are waterproof
questions.explain: Blue plasters stand out against food, making them easy to detect if they come off during preparation.

questions.q: Why should food that has been thawed not be refrozen without being cooked first?
options: Bacteria multiply while the food is thawing, and refreezing does not destroy them
Refreezing changes the food's colour
Thawed food cannot fit back in the freezer
Refreezing removes all the flavour
questions.explain: During thawing bacteria become active and multiply; freezing only makes them dormant, so refreezing raw thawed food is unsafe.

questions.q: What does a 'use-by' date on a food product tell the consumer?
options: The date after which the food may be unsafe to eat
The date after which the food simply loses its best quality but is still safe
The date the food was manufactured
The date the food should be put in the freezer
questions.explain: A use-by date relates to safety on high-risk foods, whereas a best-before date relates only to quality.

questions.q: What does the stock rotation principle 'first in, first out' (FIFO) mean in practice?
options: Older stock is placed at the front and used before newly delivered stock
The most expensive stock is sold first
Frozen food is always used before chilled food
Stock is used in a random order
questions.explain: FIFO means using older stock before newer deliveries so that food is used within its date and waste is reduced.

questions.q: Which colour of chopping board should be used for preparing raw red meat?
options: Red
Green
Blue
Yellow
questions.explain: Colour-coded boards prevent cross-contamination; the red board is used specifically for raw meat.

questions.q: A cut apple turns brown when left exposed to the air. What causes this change?
options: Enzymes in the apple reacting with oxygen
Bacteria multiplying on the surface
Mould growing on the flesh
The apple freezing
questions.explain: Enzymic browning is caused by natural enzymes in the fruit reacting with oxygen once the flesh is exposed.

questions.q: At a barbecue, chicken pieces look charred on the outside but the meat near the bone is still pink. What is the safest action?
options: Return the pieces to the heat until the juices run clear and the core reaches 75 C
Serve it immediately as the outside is well cooked
Leave it to rest, as resting will cook the middle
Add extra barbecue sauce to hide the pink colour
questions.explain: Poultry must be cooked right through to a core temperature of 75 C with clear juices to destroy bacteria such as Salmonella and Campylobacter.

questions.q: A cheese and ham sandwich has been left in a warm classroom for about five hours. What is the most sensible decision?
options: Throw it away, as bacteria will have multiplied in the danger zone
Eat it, because it still looks and smells fine
Put it in the fridge and eat it tomorrow
Warm it slightly to make it safe
questions.explain: High-risk food kept in the danger zone for several hours may contain harmful bacteria that are not made safe by chilling or gentle warming.

questions.q: You need to defrost a frozen chicken safely before cooking it tomorrow. What is the best method?
options: Defrost it fully in the fridge, on a covered plate on the bottom shelf
Leave it on the kitchen worktop overnight
Defrost it in a bowl of warm water
Cook it straight from frozen in a low oven
questions.explain: Thawing in the fridge keeps the food out of the danger zone, and covering it on the bottom shelf prevents drips contaminating other food.

questions.q: After a meal you have leftover cooked rice you want to keep. What is the correct way to store it?
options: Cool it quickly, ideally within one to two hours, then cover and refrigerate
Leave it out overnight to cool completely before storing
Put the hot rice straight into a sealed container in the fridge
Keep it in a warm oven until the next day
questions.explain: Cooling cooked rice quickly and refrigerating it limits the growth of Bacillus cereus and its heat-resistant toxin.
